title: "The posturographic sensory hierarchy, certified: sway rises monotonically Open-Firm < Closed-Firm < Open-Foam < Closed-Foam"
subtitle: "The 2×2 vision × surface balance design, tested correctly for repeated measures on 158 subjects"
categories: [posturography, balance, vision, proprioception, validated]
author: "Yusuke Matsui"
date: "2026-09-10"

> **What this case shows** — standing balance leans on vision and on proprioception (the foot/ankle sense of
> the surface). The BDS challenges both in a 2×2 design — eyes open/closed × firm/foam — measured on *every*
> subject. Because the four conditions are repeated measures, the right omnibus test is the non-parametric
> **Friedman** test. Each subject's mean COP path length per condition comes from the **certified**
> `swayMetrics`; the **newly-authored** `friedmanTest` compares the four conditions across 158 subjects,
> reproducing base R **`friedman.test`** **bit-for-bit** and **`scipy.stats.friedmanchisquare`** to machine
> precision. The conditions differ overwhelmingly (**Q(3)=420, p~1e-90**) in a **monotone** order:
> **Open-Firm < Closed-Firm < Open-Foam < Closed-Foam**.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — one `swayMetrics()` value per subject per condition → a subjects × conditions matrix → `friedmanTest()`.
**Way of thinking** — when the same people are measured under every condition, the conditions are *paired*:
use a repeated-measures test, not a between-groups one. Ranking within each subject removes between-subject
scale differences and asks the sharper question — *within a person*, which condition sways more?
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioMoCap::swayMetrics()`, `PhysioAnalysis::friedmanTest()`.
:::

## Proposition

Across 158 subjects measured under all four conditions, COP path length differs (Friedman Q=420.1 on 3 df,
p~9.7e-91) with a monotone mean-rank order Open-Firm (1.31) < Closed-Firm (1.69) < Open-Foam (3.08) <
Closed-Foam (3.92); `friedmanTest` reproduces base R `friedman.test` bit-for-bit and
`scipy.stats.friedmanchisquare` to machine precision.

## Question & goal

**The question is the sensory hierarchy and the right test for it: do the four vision × surface conditions
differ, in what order, and does the certified test reproduce the reference?** The Romberg case
([romberg-vision-sway-bds](../romberg-vision-sway-bds/index.qmd)) left open how the sensory contributions
combine across the full 2×2 design; because the conditions are within-subject, this fold answers it with the
correct repeated-measures omnibus.

## Challenge & approach

For every subject who completed all four conditions we take the mean COP path length per condition (from
`swayMetrics`, certified against the Prieto reference in the
[sway-posturography-bds](../sway-posturography-bds/index.qmd) case), assemble the 158 × 4 matrix, and test
it with `friedmanTest`, checking the omnibus Q and p against `scipy.stats.friedmanchisquare` and base R.

```
158 subjects × 4 conditions (swayMetrics path length, certified)
  mean path length (cm):  Open-Firm 60  ·  Closed-Firm 66  ·  Open-Foam 177  ·  Closed-Foam 222
  mean rank:              1.31          <  1.69           <  3.08           <  3.92
  friedmanTest → Q(3) = 420.1, p ~ 9.7e-91
     vs base R friedman.test          → |diff| = 0 (bit-for-bit)
     vs scipy.stats.friedmanchisquare → |diff| ~ 6e-14 (machine precision)
```

## Data

**Santos & Duarte (2016) BDS balance dataset (figshare)**: force-plate COP at 100 Hz, 60 s quiet standing,
2×2 vision (open/closed) × surface (firm/foam); the 158 subjects with all four conditions (complete blocks),
one per-subject mean per condition. Details in [`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: COP path length by condition (log scale, n=158) — firm ground sits near 60 cm whether the eyes are open or closed, then foam roughly triples it (177–222 cm), eyes-closed foam worst. Right: the Friedman mean ranks — a clean monotone ladder Open-Firm (1.31) → Closed-Firm (1.69) → Open-Foam (3.08) → Closed-Foam (3.92), Q(3)=420, p~1e-90.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* left — the surface dominates: softening it (foam) dwarfs closing the eyes. Right — the
rank ladder is monotone, and the steps are uneven: the firm→foam jump (~1.4 ranks) is far larger than the
open→closed jump (~0.4), so proprioception carries more of quiet standing than vision does — until the
surface is unreliable, when vision takes over (the Open-Foam → Closed-Foam step).

| Condition | mean path length (cm) | mean rank |
|---|--:|--:|
| Open-Firm | 60 | 1.31 |
| Closed-Firm | 66 | 1.69 |
| Open-Foam | 177 | 3.08 |
| Closed-Foam | 222 | 3.92 |
| **Friedman Q** (df 3) | **420.1** | |
| −log₁₀ p | 90.0 (p ~ 9.7e-91) | |
| vs base R `friedman.test` (\|diff\|) | **0** (bit-for-bit) | |
| vs `scipy.stats.friedmanchisquare` (\|diff\|) | **< 1e-9** (~6e-14) | |

The omnibus test equals base R exactly and scipy to machine precision. Values trace to
[`artifacts/sway_friedman_summary.csv`](artifacts/sway_friedman_summary.csv).

## Conclusion

`friedmanTest`, the within-subject counterpart of the certified `oneWayAnova`, reproduces the reference on
the certified `swayMetrics`. The transferable takeaway: **when the same people are measured under every
condition, rank within subject and test with Friedman. Doing so here reveals a clean sensory hierarchy —
firm ground needs little vision, foam roughly triples sway, and eyes-closed foam is worst — quantifying how
standing balance re-weights proprioception and vision as each is challenged.**

## Open questions

- The omnibus certifies the four conditions differ, in a monotone order; post-hoc pairwise tests (Nemenyi /
  Conover) would establish which specific pairs differ, and a two-way vision × surface analysis with an
  interaction term would test directly whether vision matters more on foam than on firm ground (the pattern
  the ranks suggest). The Friedman omnibus is the correct first-line repeated-measures test. *Documented,
  not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| Posturography sway metrics | `swayMetrics()` | PhysioMoCap |
| Friedman repeated-measures omnibus | `friedmanTest()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| One-way ANOVA / t-tests (between-subjects) | `oneWayAnova()`, `twoSampleTTest()` | PhysioAnalysis |

**Reading the result.**

- **mean rank** — the average within-subject rank of a condition (1 = least sway for that person); the
  ladder gives the sensory hierarchy directly.
- **repeated measures** — because every subject sees every condition, use Friedman (or repeated-measures
  ANOVA), not a between-groups test; ranking within subject cancels between-subject scale differences.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioMoCap); library(PhysioAnalysis)

# one swayMetrics path length per subject per condition -> subjects x conditions matrix M
M <- sapply(conditions, function(cnd) sapply(subjects, function(s) swayMetrics(cop[[s]][[cnd]], 100)$path_length))
friedmanTest(M)   # tie-corrected chi-square, p, df -- bit-for-bit vs base R, machine-precision vs scipy
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
[`artifacts/sway_friedman_summary.csv`](artifacts/sway_friedman_summary.csv), and [`audit.py`](audit.py)
re-checks the omnibus Q, p and df, the bit-exact match against base R and the machine-precision match against
scipy, the per-condition mean ranks and the monotone ordering, the design sizes, and the honestly noted scope
(authors the new friedmanTest op; path length from the certified swayMetrics; repeated-measures design;
cross-sectional association).
